newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ANI says no legal action over ABT purchase.
newsitem.headline: ANI says no legal action over ABT purchase.

text.p: Heavy engineering firm Australian National Industries Ltd (ANI) said on Tuesday that it had decided not to take any legal action arising from its 1991 acquisition of the German-based environmental business ABT.
ABT was acquired from Kerry Packer's Consolidated Press Holdings Group, which was then the largest shareholder in ANI.

ANI said the decision not to pursue legal action was made by its directors in response to the Ellicott report into the ABT purchase. It said it could not release the report for legal reasons but had provided the Australian Securities Commission, which used its compulsory powers, with a copy.

"The board has sought to weigh the relative merits of the possibility of recovering losses incurred by the company arising directly from the acquisition of ABT against embarking upon uncertain and protracted litigation," ANI said.

"Directors of ANI (exempting those serving at the time of the acquisition) have carefully considered the matter and unanimously decided not to commence any legal actions as a result of these investigation."
ANI said it concluded it would be in the best interest of shareholders to focus its resources on current and future activities, which include the sale of ABT and its Holter parent.
ANI said consideration of any legal action would have to include consideration of establishing facts and points of law along with estimating the size of possible damages.
The potential damages to be received would have to include a separation of how much ANI lost directly from the ABT acquisition and how much was lost by ABT following the acquisition.
ANI said while it estimated that total net losses since 1991 from ABT and Holter businesses was just under A$400 million, about 10 percent arose directly from the ABT purchase.
"Therefore, the vast majority of the losses incurred by ANI rose from post-acquisition issues and from Holter's non-ABT activities," ANI said.
It said the estimated total losses included an expected loss of A$35 million in the 1996/97 (June/July) year, of which A$18 million was reported in the first half.

The Ellicott report was commissioned in October 1996, a time when the company was embroiled in a boardroom dispute over its German operations. Ross Palmer, a dissident director who urged close investigation of the Holter operations, was voted off the board at the 1995/96 annual meeting in the same month.
The losses from the Holter group has dragged down ANI in recent years and led to a sharp fall in its share price, ending its status as a bluechip stock.
The shares, however, have recovered slowly since managing director Peter Stancliffe began a restructuring programme including asset sales in late 1996.
